claims.text: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr has a disordered BCC structure.
Approximately 1 wt.% oxygen in HfNbTaTiZr introduces local lattice distortions.
A machine-learning framework can incorporate electronic-structure, lattice-distortion, and oxygen-defect information to make temperature-dependent conductivity predictions.
The conductivity model can be calibrated using ab initio data from binary alloys and measurements of defects in oxygen-doped specimens.
The proposed framework can capture two conductivity mechanisms in bulk HfNbTaTiZr that traditional analytical models miss.
From nearly 0 to 200 K, conductivity in oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr is dominated by thermally activated hopping through defect-induced localized states.
From 300 to 1200 K, intrinsic band conduction coexists with enhanced scattering caused by oxygen-related lattice distortions.
Oxygen impurities create defect states and local lattice distortions that alter electron-scattering rates and activation energies.
At 300–1200 K, intrinsic phonon scattering is augmented by defect scattering in oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr.
Transforming raw defect and electronic features into an expandable learned representation will correlate better with measured conductivity.
Conventional analytical conductivity predictions generally assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
Conventional analytical models typically overestimate HfNbTaTiZr conductivity because they omit defect-induced scattering.
The proposed model will reduce conductivity-prediction errors by approximately 20–30% relative to analytical models.
The proposed model will closely match measured conductivity curves across both stated temperature regimes.
The prediction is restricted to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen content near 1 wt.% and to the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K intervals.
Applicability between 200 and 300 K or at substantially different oxygen concentrations is uncertain.
Temperature-dependent conductivity, Arrhenius activation energies, and lattice distortions can be measured to test the model.
The hypothesis is falsified if the model both fails to remain within ±10% of measured conductivity and fails to distinguish the two regimes more accurately than conventional analytical models.
